eyebrow: Statistics & Probability for Data Science · Chapter 5, Lesson 21
subtitle: The most reported, and most misunderstood, number in statistics.

eyebrow: The exact definition, confirmed by a real t-test
code:
t, p = stats.ttest_ind(new, old, equal_var=False)
print(round(t, 3), round(p, 4))
# 2.151  0.0346  -- matches last lesson's permutation p of 0.0343
caption: P(data this extreme | null is true) -- a statement about the data GIVEN the null.

eyebrow: What a p-value of 0.035 does NOT mean

steps.label: NOT "3.5% chance H0 is true"
steps.sub: The p-value ALREADY assumes H0 is true

steps.label: NOT "96.5% chance the effect is real"
NOT A MEASURE OF EFFECT SIZE
steps.sub: It mixes effect size with sample size

steps.label: 0.05 IS A CONVENTION
steps.sub: Not a law -- some fields need 0.01 or stricter

eyebrow: An A/A test: the null is actually true
code:
for i in range(5000):
    a = rng.normal(55, 15, 40)
    b = rng.normal(55, 15, 40)   # SAME population
    ps[i] = stats.ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False).pvalue
print((ps < 0.05).mean())   # 0.0488
caption: 5,000 repeats of a test where nothing is going on -- about 4.88% still land below 0.05.

eyebrow: p-values under a true null are UNIFORM
caption: Exactly what alpha=0.05 promises: a 5% false-alarm rate. One "win" among many tries isn't news.

eyebrow: A real but tiny effect, with huge n
code:
a = rng.normal(55.0, 15, 200_000)
b = rng.normal(55.3, 15, 200_000)
r = stats.ttest_ind(b, a, equal_var=False)
print(b.mean() - a.mean(), r.pvalue)
# 0.377  1.8e-15 -- astronomically significant
caption: But the effect is only ~0.025 standard deviations -- well under a dollar.

steps.label: ENOUGH DATA MAKES ANYTHING "SIGNIFICANT"
steps.sub: Pair p with an effect size and a CI

steps.sub: Not just whether it cleared a threshold
